analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties for wage theft and gives workers new tools to recover unpaid wages.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 26 Democratic and independent senators, was introduced June 24, 2026 and referred to the Senate labor committee, where it has received no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets wage theft — employers not paying workers everything they are owed, through unpaid minimum wage, missed overtime, off-the-clock work, or withheld tips. It would require employers to tell workers their pay rate and classification, issue itemized paystubs, and pay final wages within 14 days of a job ending. It would roughly triple the damages workers can win in court, extend the time limit to sue from 2 years to 4, ban forced arbitration of these claims, raise fines for violators to as much as $250,150 per worker for repeat violations, and fund community groups that help workers recover unpaid wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers underpay them, especially low-wage workers, temporary workers, immigrants, and women and workers of color, who the bill's findings say experience wage theft at far higher rates. Law-abiding employers also gain a level playing field against competitors that cut costs by underpaying.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal right to full compensation at the rate promised in a contract or union agreement, not just the legal minimum, and repeals the provision that lets employers escape through 'tip credit' or agreed alternatives [S2].

Requires employers to give new hires written notice of their pay rate and classification, itemized paystubs showing hours, rates, and deductions, and all final wages within 14 days of termination — with daily pay for each day a final payment is late [S2].

Raises damages from an equal 'liquidated' amount to 2x unpaid wages plus interest in most cases and 3x for repeat violators, and raises maximum civil fines to $25,150 per worker per initial violation and $250,150 for willful or repeated violations [S2].

Doubles the window to sue (from 2 years to 4, or 5 for willful violations), suspends the clock while the Labor Department investigates, bars employers from forcing workers into arbitration agreements that waive their right to sue, and creates a rebuttable presumption in workers' favor when employers have failed to keep records [S2].

Requires the Labor Department to refer record-falsifying willful offenders to the Justice Department for prosecution, with criminal fines raised to $100,000 per affected worker, and authorizes grants through 2030 to nonprofits, unions, and community groups that help workers recover back pay [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that underpay workers — through higher damages, fines, and litigation risk — and compliant employers who face new recordkeeping, paystub, and disclosure costs. Taxpayers fund the grant program.

drawbacks.text: Higher penalties, expanded damages, and a longer time to sue raise the cost and risk of litigation for employers, including those with honest bookkeeping disputes, and small businesses with limited payroll staff bear the new paystub, notice, and 14-day final-pay requirements [S2].
The grant program is funded by 'such sums as may be necessary' without a set budget, and the changes to damages and enforcement will shift disputes from flexible arbitration to federal court [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers are large and concrete: the bill's own findings cite an estimated $50 billion a year stolen from workers and note that in some industries fewer than half of employers comply with wage law [S2]. The costs are real but mostly fall on employers that are violating the law or that must set up routine pay transparency they lack in many states; the administrative burden on small compliant businesses is the strongest honest objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has not scheduled any hearing or vote, and the congressional session still has months to run.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced S. 4919 with 25 Democratic and independent cosponsors on June 24, 2026 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, and no further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — has been taken [S4].
None of the 26 sponsors is a Republican, so the bill has no bipartisan cosponsorship [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change anything: employers facing wage-and-hour claims are better off that the bill has not advanced, while workers continue to bear the estimated $50 billion a year in unpaid wages that the bill was written to address [S2].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers facing wage claims, so far

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 25 Democratic and independent cosponsors; chairs matters before the committee it was referred to.

for.name: 25 Senate cosponsors (24 Democrats, 1 independent)
for.role: Cosponsors including Sanders, Warren, Baldwin, Booker, Markey
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since its referral on June 24, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican senator has cosponsored, and the bill has not yet reached a vote.

industries.industry: Employers with histories of wage-and-hour violations (restaurants, retail, construction, agriculture, staffing agencies)
industries.note: They face up to $250,150 per worker in fines, triple damages, criminal referral for falsified records, and a longer window to be sued, all aimed at recovering the estimated $50 billion a year workers lose to underpayment [S2].

industries.industry: Forced arbitration providers and employers relying on arbitration agreements
industries.note: The bill bars employers from waiving workers' right to bring wage claims in court through pre-dispute arbitration agreements, keeping disputes in open court or class actions [S2].
They bear new paystub, disclosure, recordkeeping, and 14-day final pay obligations, but the bill also protects them from competitors that underpay workers to undercut their prices [S2].

industries.industry: Nonprofits, labor unions, and community organizations
industries.note: They are eligible for Labor Department grants to educate workers, help file claims, and partner on enforcement through 2030 [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic sponsorship and no committee action on the calendar in a Congress controlled so that labor bills of this kind rarely reach the floor, the most likely path is that the bill stays in the HELP committee until the session ends in January 2027 without a vote, dying when the session ends; the next step would be a committee hearing or markup, which no source shows is planned.
